Ceylon. The island nation's name during British colonial rule derived from Portuguese and Dutch corruption of the Sanskrit word Ceilao. Upon gaining independence in nineteen-forty-eight, the nation gradually transitioned to Sri Lanka, meaning blessed island or resplendent island in Sinhalese and Sanskrit. The formal adoption came in nineteen-seventy-two as part of a new republican constitution, representing a return to the island's indigenous heritage and a break from colonial nomenclature.

The name Ceylon traces back to sixteenth-century Portuguese transliteration of indigenous names, a transliteration that persisted through Dutch and British rule. Britain colonized Ceylon in seventeen-ninety-six after ousting the Dutch, making it a crown jewel of the Raj. British planters developed extensive tea and rubber plantations, transforming the island's economy. When Sri Lanka was officially adopted in nineteen-seventy-two, it replaced both the colonial name and the title Dominion of Ceylon.

The island's Sinhalese majority comprises about seventy-five percent of the population, with Tamil minorities concentrated in the north. The name change elevated Sinhalese cultural identity. Ceylon was long a major center of Theravada Buddhism and home to the sacred Temple of the Tooth in Kandy, a place of pilgrimage for Buddhists across Asia. The transition from Ceylon to Sri Lanka symbolized postcolonial assertion, though the nation would face civil conflict between Sinhalese and Tamil communities from nineteen-eighty-three through twenty-oh-nine. Despite this struggle, the nation's Buddhist heritage and Sinhalese language remain central to the modern identity of Sri Lanka.
